children: The proposed BESS mandate comes as battery makers look beyond electric mobility towards stationary energy storage.

The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has proposed making battery energy storage systems (BESS) mandatory for all new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned from 1 July 2027, a move that could accelerate the battery industry's shift beyond electric mobility into stationary storage.

Under the draft rules, a 100 MW solar or wind project would need at least 10 MW of storage capacity with a minimum two-hour duration. The requirement would rise to four hours for projects commissioned from July 2029.

The proposal comes as India's need for grid-scale storage is expected to expand sharply. The country added 2,668.54 MW of BESS power capacity, equivalent to 7,785.6 MWh of storage in 2026. Solar capacity stood at 164.59 GW and wind at 58.14 GW as of 31 July.

For battery manufacturers that built their businesses largely around electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and light commercial vehicles, the emerging stationary-storage market offers another major source of demand.
A Formalisation, Not A Surprise

The proposed mandate largely formalises a transition that is already visible in procurement. “Buyers have stopped asking for vanilla solar in the last few months — every serious conversation in the last months has been peak-power or solar-plus-storage,” said Sudharman Ezhil, Director & CEO, Natrinai Ventures (NGE Green Energy).

Ezhil said storage makes renewable assets more useful to lenders and offtakers by allowing projects to schedule power, manage deviation settlement and participate in evening demand periods, when time-of-day tariffs and exchange prices can be significantly higher than daytime solar rates. it's a welcome move,” he said.

Ezhil expects storage to become standard within two to three years, irrespective of the mandate, as buyers look for projects that can provide power beyond solar generation hours. NGE Green, for instance, already treats BESS as a default line item. The system is sized according to the offtaker's load rather than the regulatory minimum.
Beyond Electric Mobility

The emerging BESS market is also allowing lithium-ion battery manufacturers to diversify beyond electric mobility. Pratik Kamdar, Co-founder & CEO, Neuron Energy, said BESS “has the potential to become a significant new market for Indian lithium-ion battery manufacturers”, pointing to India's projected requirement of more than 236 GWh of BESS by 2031-32.
“This creates an opportunity to diversify beyond electric mobility and participate in utility-scale as well as commercial and industrial storage applications,” Kamdar said.

The shift is also beginning to appear in manufacturers' strategies. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility told investors after its FY26 results that it was giving BESS a larger role in its mix. “A major change in our strategy is the introduction of BESS as a larger part of our mix. Earlier, we had largely focused on EVs,” the company's management said.
For manufacturers, the opportunity extends beyond cells and battery packs to areas such as battery management systems, thermal management and monitoring technologies.
Same Cells, Different Engineering

The move into stationary storage, however, is not a straightforward extension of EV battery manufacturing. “BESS cannot be treated as a simple extension of an EV battery platform,” Kamdar said, pointing to differences in operating requirements, including long-duration operation and frequent charge-discharge cycles.
“Battery pack architecture, BMS software, monitoring and thermal-management systems need to be designed around the specific operating profile of stationary storage,” Kamdar added.

At the same time, the underlying expertise developed through EV battery manufacturing remains transferable, giving existing lithium-ion manufacturers a starting point as they move into grid-scale and commercial storage.
Regulatory Gaps Persist
While the market opportunity is expanding, developers point to commercial and regulatory issues that could affect the pace of deployment.

Ezhil said one challenge is the way solar-plus-storage projects are priced. “The industry keeps trying to sell a blended Rs /kWh tariff that folds battery costs into solar energy. That structure fails bankability,” he said.

Ezhil argued that solar and storage need separate capacity and energy charges, or that batteries should be deployed behind the meter, to better reflect the different functions and costs of the two assets.
State-level rules also remain inconsistent, particularly around banking and surcharge provisions for commercial and industrial storage projects, Ezhil said.

Tamil Nadu's resource adequacy plan, for instance, projects a need for more than 11 GW of additional storage by 2035 and flags evening-hour power shortages between October and April. “The regulatory framework should be pulling private storage into that gap, and we are waiting eagerly for the new policy to get going,” Ezhil said.
The CEA has invited comments on its draft proposal until 4 October 2026, before the regulations are finalised.

For India's battery manufacturers, the proposed mandate could provide further impetus for stationary storage to develop from a supplementary market into a significant part of the country's power infrastructure.
